assetPricing.title: Asset Pricing
assetPricing.intro: 21 interactive tools: from no-arbitrage foundations (state prices · risk-neutral measure · SDF-factor duality · HJ distance) through equilibrium pricing (CAPM · zero-beta · ICAPM), factors and empirics (APT · Fama-French · Fama-MacBeth · anomaly sorts · GRS), the modern SDF framework, and on to structural puzzles (long-run risk · habit formation · rare disasters) and the empirical frontier (Campbell-Shiller decomposition · factor zoo · currency carry).

frontier.chartNote: Rᶠ = 2% · click a point on the gold frontier to see its weights · diamond = GMV · star = tangency portfolio · dashed = CML
frontier.diversificationSub: Risk reduction (GMV vs equal-weight average volatility)
frontier.pySigma: # Σ built from each asset's σ and correlation ρ={{rho}}

zerobeta.chartHint: Black (1972): when risk-free borrowing is unavailable, the zero-beta return E(Rz) replaces Rf. Since E(Rz)>Rf the SML intercept rises and its slope flattens — exactly the empirical pattern of high low-β returns and low high-β returns.
zerobeta.n1: Relaxes the risk-free asset assumption. The zero-beta portfolio is the minimum-variance portfolio uncorrelated with the market.
zerobeta.n2: Rf is replaced by E(Rz), typically with E(Rz)>Rf.
zerobeta.n3: Explains the flatter-than-theory SML documented by Black-Jensen-Scholes (1972).

icapm.n1: E(Ri)−Rf = βim·λm + Σ βih·λh; extra factors arise from hedging shifts in the investment opportunity set.
icapm.n2: Assets that pay off when the opportunity set deteriorates provide hedging value and can command a lower (or higher) premium.
icapm.n3: With λh=0 it collapses to the CAPM; with λh≠0 it gives a theoretical basis for multi-factor models (FF3/FF5, q-factors).

stateprice.chart: State prices q, physical π, risk-neutral Q and SDF m = q/π
stateprice.chartHint: The risk-neutral measure simply folds “bad states are expensive” into the probabilities: Q is inflated relative to π in bad states, and the ratio is exactly (1+Rf)·m.
stateprice.n1: P = Σ q·X = E[m·X] with m = q/π. No arbitrage ⇔ a strictly positive state-price vector exists; completeness ⇔ the payoff matrix has full rank (rank = S).
stateprice.n2: Under incompleteness any price inside [lower, upper] is arbitrage-free; pinning down a unique price requires equilibrium, preferences or frictions.

duality.maxSharpeSub: the flip side of the HJ bound
duality.chartHint: b = Σ⁻¹λ/E(m) projects factor premia into pricing-kernel loadings. The beta and SDF-covariance representations agree numerically — a linear factor model is just the SDF projected onto the factor space.
duality.n1: m = E[m] − b'(f − E f), with b = Σ_f⁻¹ λ / E[m].
duality.n2: So “finding factors” and “finding the pricing kernel” are the same exercise: APT / Fama-French regressions restrict m to the span of the factors.

hjdist.chart: Model comparison: HJ distance / mean |α| / cross-sectional R²
hjdist.chartHint: The HJ distance measures how far a candidate SDF sits from a valid pricing kernel; unlike GRS it is not inflated by sample length, which makes it well suited to cross-model comparison.
hjdist.chart2: Pricing errors α across test portfolios
hjdist.chart2Hint: A monotone spread of positive and negative α means the model omits a systematic factor aligned with that sort.
hjdist.n1: Workflow: run time-series regressions for α → weight by the second-moment matrix E[RR′] → δ = √(α′E[RR′]⁻¹α). Smaller δ means the candidate SDF prices all test assets more accurately.
hjdist.n2: δ vs GRS: GRS is a statistical test (is α significantly nonzero?), the HJ distance is an economic measure (how much money is mispriced?). With long samples GRS rejects almost surely, while δ stays comparable.

backtest.noteMeanrev: z = (rₜ - MA)/SD, reverse when z exceeds threshold.
backtest.notePairs: spread = log(P₂/P₁), OU process dz = -κz·dt + σ·dW, long/short the spread.
backtest.noteCost: All strategies include two-sided transaction costs and daily mark-to-market.

bl.view1: View 1: US Equity vs EU Equity (relative)
bl.framework: Derive implied equilibrium returns π = δΣw_mkt from CAPM, then Bayesian-update with views (P, Q, Ω).
bl.confNote: Higher confidence → smaller Ω → posterior closer to views; τ controls prior dispersion.

ff.alphaNote: Significant positive α → genuine skill; if |t_α| < 2, α is indistinguishable from zero.

walkforward.equityChartTitle: Out-of-Sample Equity — Walk-Forward Strategy vs Buy & Hold
walkforward.foldsChartTitle: Per-Fold IS vs OOS Sharpe — Out-of-Sample Decay
walkforward.noteWf: Roll parameter selection over the IS window, evaluate only on the immediately following OOS window, and stitch together all OOS segments for a look-ahead-free performance estimate.
walkforward.noteOverfit: A full-sample optimal Sharpe much higher than OOS (large gap) signals overfitting; with pure noise (φ=0), OOS should fall back near 0.

riskparity.rcChartTitle: Risk Contribution Decomposition (%) — ERC should be near-flat
riskparity.ercNote: Weights satisfy wᵢ·(Σw)ᵢ = const ⇒ each asset contributes equally to portfolio variance.
riskparity.hrpNote: Avoids inverting Σ⁻¹, more robust to noisy covariances; hierarchical clustering sidesteps Markowitz ill-conditioning.
riskparity.rcNote: In the risk-contribution bar chart, ERC is nearly flat → balanced risk; Min-Var concentrates heavily on low-σ assets.

bl.noteConf: c→0 views vanish back to π; c→1 views are fully embedded.
bl.noteTau: Higher prior uncertainty gives views more weight and a stronger posterior deviation.

cvar.noteRU: min ζ + 1/((1-α)S) Σ (−rᵀw − ζ)⁺, solved via projected subgradient with long-only constraint.
cvar.noteIntuition: Under fat-tail scenarios, CVaR optimization more markedly reduces weights on high-volatility / high-tail-risk assets.

shrink.noteLambda: Σ̂ = λF + (1−λ)S; smaller T/N gives larger λ.
shrink.noteEffect: Condition number drops, and out-of-sample variance forecast error for min-var / MV / RP improves accordingly.

resamp.chartWeights: Mean ± Volatility of Weights at Median Target (%)
resamp.noteMichaud: Resample (μ̂,Σ̂) → frontier → average aligned by quantile, resolving over-concentrated "corner solutions".

factor.noteFormula: Var(w) = wᵀ B F Bᵀ w + wᵀ D w
factor.noteFormulaRest: ; solved via projected subgradient so factor risk contributions match target budgets.
factor.noteExposure: Factor exposure β_p = Bᵀw; used for factor neutralization or active factor tilting.

kelly.chartTerminal: Terminal Wealth Distribution: Median and 5%/95% Quantiles
kelly.noteFrac: g(f) = f·(μ_p − r_f) + r_f − ½ f²σ_p². Full Kelly maximizes long-run growth, but short-term drawdown and ruin probability are significant.
kelly.noteAdvice: Half Kelly typically sacrifices little growth while substantially reducing ruin probability.

geometry.smlPanelTitle: Security Market Line — benchmarked to the tangency portfolio
geometry.note1: : any frontier portfolio is a linear combination of GMV and another frontier portfolio; once a risk-free asset is introduced, every investor only needs r_f and the tangency portfolio, with risk preference determining position along the CAL.
geometry.note2a: Setting the leverage cap to 1 (no borrowing) truncates the CAL at the tangency point; the equilibrium pricing reference is then no longer r_f but the
geometry.note2b: — Black's (1972) zero-beta CAPM, which raises the SML intercept and flattens its slope.
geometry.note3: The long-only frontier always sits to the lower-right of the unconstrained frontier: constraints are both an investment view and an implicit regularization against estimation error.

singleIndex.preset1Desc: N=25, T=48 → sample covariance breaks down
singleIndex.oosPanelTitle: Out-of-sample true volatility — min-variance portfolios from each covariance estimate
singleIndex.note1: Mean absolute covariance error: sample {{sample}} vs single-index {{index}}.
singleIndex.note2a: Sharpe's (1963) single-index model compresses N(N+1)/2 free parameters into 2N+1:
singleIndex.note2b: , at the cost of assuming uncorrelated residuals. Multi-factor models offer a further bias-variance tradeoff.
singleIndex.note3: Structured estimation only pays off when T is small relative to N; once the sample is long enough, sample covariance's lower bias wins out.

estimationError.preset1Desc: N=8, T=60 → 1/N is hard to beat
estimationError.tablePanelTitle: Out-of-sample (true-parameter) annualized Sharpe — Monte Carlo mean
estimationError.oracleNote: Theoretical upper bound: no estimation rule can beat it
estimationError.note1a: Estimation error in the mean vector is far larger than in covariance: this is why min-variance portfolios are often more stable than tangency portfolios, and why
estimationError.note2: Plug-in optimization mistakes noise for signal: assets with the largest estimation error tend to receive the most extreme weights — the "error maximizer" effect.
estimationError.note3: Three remedies: shrinkage estimation (Ledoit-Wolf), Bayesian priors (Black-Litterman), and direct constraints/regularization — this section has a tool for each.

rebalance.preset2Desc: 80bp cost, a wider band is better
rebalance.tablePanelTitle: Rebalancing rule comparison (5-yr simulation, 6-asset equal-weight target)
rebalance.tradeoffPanelTitle: Cost — tracking error tradeoff curve (threshold bands)
rebalance.driftPanelTitle: Weight drift path and trigger band
rebalance.capPanelTitle: Effect of weight caps on the min-variance solution
rebalance.note1a: Rebalancing is not about "returning to target weights" but
rebalance.note1Bold: trading transaction cost for control of risk exposure
rebalance.note1b: : calendar rules are simple and auditable; threshold rules automatically tighten in volatile periods and relax in calm ones.
rebalance.note2: Not rebalancing lets a portfolio drift toward whichever asset has recently risen most — effectively passive momentum exposure, with its risk profile drifting away from the target.
rebalance.note3: Weight caps are both a compliance constraint and an implicit regularizer: they raise the effective number of assets, at the cost of higher in-sample volatility for the min-variance solution.

active.gridPanelTitle: Fundamental law: IR grows with the square root of breadth
active.note1b: . Raising breadth is usually more realistic than improving forecast accuracy, but "independent" is the key word — 500 highly correlated stocks are not 500 independent bets.
active.note2: Value added IR²/(4λ) and optimal tracking error IR/(2λ) imply: without skill you shouldn't take active risk; the active risk budget should be set by skill, not ambition.
active.note3: Treynor-Black uses the ratio of α to residual risk (appraisal ratio) as the sole basis for position sizing: combined Sharpe² = market Sharpe² + appraisal ratio².

downside.preset1Desc: B has higher return but left-tail jumps
downside.cdfPanelTitle: Cumulative distribution and its integral (SSD criterion)
downside.ceqPanelTitle: CRRA certainty equivalent — optimal A weight {{v}}
downside.note1a: Variance treats upside and downside equally;
downside.note1b: penalizes only outcomes below target τ, with n=0/1/2 corresponding to loss probability, expected shortfall and semi-variance.
downside.note2: Second-order stochastic dominance requires no specific utility function beyond risk aversion — far more robust than Sharpe ranking, but it often gives the honest answer "cannot be ranked".
downside.note3: The mean-variance approximation μ − ½γσ² nearly coincides with the CRRA certainty equivalent when returns are close to normal; once left-tail jumps are introduced, the optimal points of the two curves diverge noticeably.

dynamic.preset2Desc: 3-year horizon, close to the myopic solution
dynamic.horizonPanelTitle: Term structure: myopic demand + hedging demand
dynamic.pathPanelTitle: Path dependence: annual rebalance vs. buy and hold (terminal quantiles)
dynamic.note1a: Merton (1969, 1971): under iid returns and CRRA utility, the optimal proportion
dynamic.note1b: is independent of horizon — "the young should hold more equities" requires additional assumptions to hold.
dynamic.note2a: Once the risk premium is predictable (mean-reverting), the optimal solution gains an
dynamic.note2b: ; negative correlation (premium rises as prices fall) leads long-horizon investors to hold more risky assets.
dynamic.note3: The serious justification for a lifecycle glide path is human capital: the higher the bond-like share of human capital, the more aggressive the financial portfolio should be, naturally de-risking with age.
dynamic.note4: Rebalancing and buy-and-hold produce different terminal distributions along the same path: the former compresses tail dispersion and controls risk drift, the latter amplifies winners and skews the terminal distribution to the right.

regularization.preset2Desc: λ₁=0.05, only a few positions remain
regularization.tablePanelTitle: Out-of-sample performance of regularization schemes (evaluated at true parameters)
regularization.pathPanelTitle: L1 regularization path: gross exposure and effective N
regularization.note1a: DeMiguel et al. (2009) show that imposing norm constraints on weights is equivalent to shrinking the covariance matrix —
regularization.note1b: , with long-only being the crudest but most robust form.
regularization.note2: L1 produces sparse solutions (implementable, interpretable, low trading cost); L2 pushes weights toward equal-weight (stable but diluted); combining the two gives an elastic net.
regularization.note3b: , equivalent to solving min-variance on the correlation matrix and rescaling by volatility, naturally avoiding crowded high-correlation trades.

backtestLab.title: Portfolio Backtesting & Optimization Engine
backtestLab.subtitle: Backtest single-asset strategies or multi-asset portfolios on real historical prices: single-asset supports dual moving average / momentum / mean reversion / volatility targeting with trading costs and slippage; portfolios support equal weight / risk parity / minimum variance / mean-variance with periodic rebalancing. Signals execute T+1 to avoid look-ahead bias, parameter grid scans visualize robust regions, and results can be sent to the pricing tool with one click.

qlibLab.title: Qlib Research Pipeline Lab
qlibLab.subtitle: Reproduce a full research workflow following Microsoft Qlib: Alpha158-style expression factors → cross-sectional normalization → model fitting → IC / RankIC evaluation → TopK-Dropout portfolio backtest. Training and testing are strictly split by time; all metrics are out-of-sample.

ridge.label: Ridge Linear Model
ridge.desc: Minimizes prediction error with L2 penalty on the training window, corresponding to Qlib's LinearModel.

equal.label: Equal-Weight Combination
equal.desc: Sum of z-scored factors with equal weights, used as a no-learning control benchmark.

single.label: Single Factor
single.desc: Uses only the first checked factor, to observe the information content of a single alpha.

qlibLab.poolDesc: The universe is synthesized from a market factor, momentum continuation, and weak mean reversion; the structure is learnable but with signal-to-noise close to real cross-sectional data.
qlibLab.factorWeightHint: The number in the top-right corner is the factor's weight in the model (Ridge coefficient / equal weight). At least one factor must be kept.
qlibLab.needFactor: Please check at least one factor, or increase historical days to get enough cross-sectional samples.
qlibLab.monotonicHint: Monotonic increase indicates the signal is ordered across the whole cross-section, not just effective in the tails.
qlibLab.howToRead: How to read: first check RankIC and bucket monotonicity to see if the signal holds, then check whether the equity curve beats the equal-weight benchmark. If IC is positive but equity lags, the issue is usually turnover and costs rather than the factor itself; try reducing n_drop or lengthening the rebalance interval to verify.

minvar.desc: Minimizes portfolio variance under long-only constraints.

meanvar.label: Mean-Variance
meanvar.desc: Tangency portfolio Σ⁻¹μ, projected onto the long-only simplex.

notes.qrBody: min Σ ρ<sub>τ</sub>(y − Xβ), where ρ<sub>τ</sub>(u) = u·(τ − 1{u<0}).
notes.olsVsQr: OLS fits E[Y|X], QR fits Q<sub>τ</sub>(Y|X). Under <u>heteroscedasticity</u>, β<sub>τ</sub> changes with τ — information invisible to OLS.
notes.irls: This tool uses Schlossmacher (1973) IRLS (Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares) for solving (for teaching purposes, equivalent to simplex).

quantilereg.slopeChartNote: If the β₁(τ) curve varies with τ ⇒ presence of <u>heteroscedasticity</u> or location-scale dependence; if it aligns with the OLS horizontal line ⇒ homoscedasticity, OLS and QR are equivalent.

stdLogit.name: Standard Logit
stdLogit.desc: Moderate sample size, strong x1 effect

probitDgp.name: Probit DGP
probitDgp.desc: Data generated by a Probit process

rareEvent.name: Rare Event
rareEvent.desc: Negative intercept, low share of y=1

logitprobit.coefNote: Note: Logit and Probit coefficients are not directly comparable due to different scales; compare marginal effects instead. Rule of thumb: Logit β̂ ≈ 1.6 × Probit β̂.
logitprobit.marginalEffectsNote: AME = (1/n)Σᵢ f(xᵢ'β)·βₖ; MEM = f(x̄'β)·βₖ. LPM coefficients are direct marginal effects, usually close to AME (often used as a quick approximation).
logitprobit.predictedProbNote: LPM often exceeds the [0,1] interval at the ends (truncated here); Logit and Probit curves overlap significantly, showing minimal fitting differences.

takeaways.linkFnBody: Logit uses the logistic CDF Λ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), while Probit uses the standard normal CDF Φ(z). They differ in tail behavior (Logit has fatter tails).
takeaways.whyNotOlsBody: Heteroskedasticity; predicted probabilities can fall outside [0,1]; constant marginal effects assumption is often unrealistic.
takeaways.marginalBody: β̂ coefficients lack direct scale meaning; AME or MEM are needed to quantify how a 1-unit increase in x affects the probability (in percentage points).
takeaways.mleBody: Estimated via Newton-Raphson (IRLS) iteration to solve ∂L/∂β = 0; standard errors come from the diagonal of the inverse Fisher Information Matrix I(β̂)⁻¹.
takeaways.pseudoR2Body: 1 − ll(full) / ll(intercept-only); values between 0.2-0.4 indicate a strong fit in discrete choice models.

risk.subtitle: From VaR and extreme-value tails to credit, liquidity spirals, Basel capital and recovery planning.

evt.comparisonTitle: Tail risk comparison — Normal vs Historical vs EVT (POT)
evt.comparisonNote: The normal method typically understates tail risk at 99.9%; EVT extrapolates extreme quantiles more accurately by fitting the exceedance distribution.
evt.meanExcessTitle: Mean excess plot e(u) — linearity supports the GPD
evt.tailFitTitle: Tail fit — empirical vs GPD survival function

notes.potText: Exceedances above a high threshold u follow a Generalized Pareto Distribution GPD(ξ, β) (Pickands–Balkema–de Haan theorem).
notes.xiText: ξ>0 indicates a heavy tail (Fréchet), governing extreme-quantile extrapolation; EVT is more robust than normal/historical methods at extreme confidence levels such as 99.9%.

explain.parametricText: VaR = V·(z·σ_h − μ_h); fast to compute but assumes normality, underestimating tail risk.
explain.historicalText: Uses the empirical quantile of historical returns—distribution-free but sample-dependent (here a Student-t distribution simulates fat tails).
explain.monteCarloText: Simulates random paths; flexible but computationally intensive.
explain.esText: The average loss beyond VaR; satisfies subadditivity and is more robust than VaR.

chart.title: Monte Carlo Loss Distribution and VaR Threshold
chart.footnote: The red region marks tail losses exceeding the Monte Carlo VaR. Fat-tailed historical simulation VaR/ES is typically higher than the normal parametric method, highlighting how the normality assumption understates tail risk.

chart.timeseriesTitle: Loss Time Series — VaR Line / ES Line / Breach Points
chart.histogramTitle: Loss Distribution & Tail — Red Bins Contain Breaches

footer.teachingPoint: FRTB uses ES (97.5%) instead of VaR (99%) as the capital measurement benchmark, because VaR is not subadditive and ignores tail shape.
footer.fatTailNote: When true P&L is fat-tailed (df↓), VaR under the Normal assumption is systematically underestimated → Kupiec POF rejects H₀.
footer.independenceNote: The Christoffersen independence test identifies breach clustering via a 2×2 transition matrix (clustering = model reacts too slowly to volatility changes).

stats.wwrDeltaSub: Difference between ρ≠0 and naive case

explain.wwr: Wrong-way risk: when default intensity λ_C is positively correlated with the interest rate r, defaults are more likely to occur at times of large exposure → CVA is significantly amplified.
explain.bcva: BCVA = CVA − DVA (Hull-White 2012): the bank's own default losses that are not paid out offset part of the CVA.

explain.vasicekFormula: X_i = √ρ·M + √(1−ρ)·ε_i, default occurs when X_i ≤ Φ⁻¹(PD).
explain.tCopula: The t-Copula introduces a common scale factor W ~ χ²_df/df, producing strong tail dependence → extreme joint default probabilities rise significantly, a key driver of the excess losses in the 2008 crisis.
explain.baselIrb: The Basel II IRB formula is derived from the Vasicek large-portfolio limit: K = LGD·[Φ((Φ⁻¹(PD)+√ρ·Φ⁻¹(0.999))/√(1−ρ)) − PD].

coherence.riskMeasureSpectrum: Risk Measure Spectrum — Different scales under same loss distribution (%)
coherence.coherenceNote: Red = Incoherent (VaR lacks subadditivity); Gold = Satisfies monotonicity, translation invariance, positive homogeneity, and subadditivity.
coherence.spectralWeights: Spectral Weights φ(u) — Higher values indicate more focus on the tail
coherence.elicitabilityPinball: Elicitability — Pinball score minimized at true quantile (×10⁻⁴)
coherence.axiomsDescription: Monotonicity, subadditivity, positive homogeneity, and translation invariance (Artzner et al. 1999). VaR generally fails subadditivity, so diversification may 'appear' to increase risk.
coherence.elicitabilityDescription: VaR is elicitably by pinball score alone; ES is not. However, (VaR, ES) are jointly elicitable (Fissler-Ziegel), which is why FRTB uses VaR backtesting alongside ES measurement.

vol.conditionalVolComparison: Conditional Volatility Comparison — EWMA / GARCH(1,1) / HAR (%)
vol.fhsDescription: Normalizes historical returns using GARCH conditional volatility to obtain z_t, then bootstraps and rescales by current σ_{t+1}. Combines 'heavy-tailed non-parametric shape' with 'volatility clustering'.
vol.whyStaticFailsDescription: Samples from calm periods underestimate crisis risk, while post-crisis samples overestimate it for too long—risk measures must be conditional.

irb.irbRiskWeightFunction: IRB Risk Weight Function — K(PD) vs Correlation R(PD)
irb.procyclicality: Procyclicality — Impact of Macro State z on PIT PD and RWA
irb.regulatoryCapitalElNote: Regulatory Capital covers Unexpected Loss only:
irb.elNoteDescription: EL is absorbed by provisions and pricing. K = LGD·[Φ((Φ⁻¹(PD)+√R Φ⁻¹(0.999))/√(1−R)) − PD] × Maturity Adjustment. RWA = 12.5·K·EAD.
irb.procyclicalTrapDescription: PIT PD spikes during recessions → RWA rises → Capital tightens → Credit shrinks. This is what Countercyclical Buffers and TTC ratings aim to mitigate.

migration.heavyRightSkewNote: Severely right-skewed loss distribution: the fundamental difference between credit and market risk; mean-variance fails here.
migration.thresholdModelDescription: Maps rating migration to latents x = √ρ·m + √(1−ρ)·ε; single factor m creates correlation; default is simply the worst rating grade.
migration.generatorDescription: Allows consistent interpolation of the annual matrix to any horizon, ensuring zero row sums and non-negative off-diagonals (JLT regularization).

funding.deleveragingSpiralTitle: Deleveraging Spiral — Equity, Sales, and Price
funding.twoSpiralsDescription: Loss spiral (losses → passive leverage rise → fire sales) and margin spiral (rising haircuts → reduced funding capacity → fire sales), reinforcing each other (Brunnermeier & Pedersen 2009).
funding.insightDescription: Liquidity risk cannot be expressed by a single VaR; funding structure, collateral quality, and market depth must all be considered.

basel.capitalStackTitle: Capital Stack — Required vs Actual (% RWA)
basel.threeLegsDescription: Risk-weighted capital, non-risk-weighted leverage, and liquidity ratios (LCR/NSFR)—none of these alone are sufficient to describe resilience.
basel.mdaDescription: Maximum Distributable Amount restricts dividends and bonuses once buffers are eroded, turning capital constraints into automated mechanisms.

model.sampleLengthVsUncertainty: Sample Length vs Estimation Uncertainty (Relative Spread %)
model.modelRiskGovernanceThreeLines: Model Risk Governance — Three Lines of Defense (SR 11-7 / OCC 2011-12)
model.robustCriterionDescription: ρ_ε = (1−ε)·ρ_baseline + ε·ρ_stress, used to translate 'model uncertainty' into a capital buffer rather than just picking one number.
model.modelAsRiskSourceDescription: Under Knightian uncertainty, the dispersion band itself is decision-useful; larger dispersion calls for lower leverage and higher buffers rather than parameter fine-tuning.

resilience.capitalTrajectoryTitle: Capital Trajectory — CET1 Ratio vs Trigger Line (%)
resilience.resilienceDescription: The key lies in the loss absorption hierarchy (earnings → dividend cuts → buffers → minimums) and the timeliness of management actions.
resilience.procyclicalityDescription: Buffers must be built in good times and released in crises to avoid the paradox of capital requirements being tightest when they are hardest to meet.

behavior.title: Behavioral Finance Lab
behavior.subtitle: From prospect theory and myopic loss aversion to the BSV / DHS / Hong-Stein belief models, limits to arbitrage, investor sentiment and behavioral corporate finance — eight interactive experiments turning bounded rationality into reproducible price paths.

cpt.title: Cumulative Prospect Theory: value function, probability weighting and the fourfold pattern
cpt.desc: v(x) is defined relative to a reference point: concave for gains, convex for losses, steeper on the loss side (λ>1); w(p) overweights small and underweights moderate-to-high probabilities. Together they produce the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes, explaining why lotteries and insurance coexist.

chart.value: Value function v(x) vs linear utility

note.label: Limitations:
note.text: The reference point r is neither directly observable nor exogenous; different reference points yield very different predictions. Attributing every reluctance to cut losses to loss aversion ignores rational explanations such as taxes, trading costs, private information and learning.

mla.title: Myopic loss aversion and the equity premium puzzle
mla.desc: Benartzi-Thaler: combining loss aversion λ with evaluation frequency endogenously produces a high required return on equities. The more often you evaluate, the more likely you see a loss and the higher the psychological cost — a behavioral explanation of the equity premium puzzle.

chart.utility: Prospect utility vs premium (zero crossing = equilibrium premium)

note.label: Debate:
note.text: Evaluation frequency is unobservable and long-horizon investors need not settle daily; whether differences in evaluation periods between institutions and retail investors actually map into prices remains disputed.

bsv.title: BSV: conservatism + representativeness → underreaction then overreaction
bsv.desc: Investors believe earnings switch between a mean-reverting and a trending regime. Conservatism causes underreaction at announcement followed by slow drift; representativeness extrapolates streaks of good news, pushing prices past fundamentals before a long-run reversal.

chart.car: Post-event cumulative abnormal return (CAR) vs rational baseline

note.label: Testing:
note.text: BSV's falsifiable implication is cross-sectional — drift and reversal should be stronger for stocks with vaguer information and less analyst coverage. That is what separates it from risk-premium explanations.

dhs.title: DHS: overconfidence and self-attribution bias
dhs.desc: Investors overestimate private-signal precision (k>1), causing immediate overreaction; self-attribution lets confirming public news further strengthen beliefs (continued momentum), until public information eventually pulls prices back to fundamentals — long-run reversal.

hs.title: Slow information diffusion + momentum traders: a unified explanation
hs.desc: News diffuses gradually to news-watchers over z periods, creating natural underreaction; momentum traders follow the past j-period trend, amplifying underreaction into overshoot and eventual reversal. No individual-level cognitive bias is required.
